title: How Much Car Can You Afford?
summary: The 20/4/10 rule for car budgeting no longer works at today’s prices. Here’s the 20/5/15 rule: 20% down, five years max, and 15% of gross income for all car costs.
body_markdown:
Whether you're buying new or new-to-you, the first and generally most important question is how much car you can actually afford. That number sets the stage for every decision after it: whether you purchase new or used, which segment you shop in, and which features or trim levels make the cut.

## What is the 20/5/15 rule?


Financial advisors offer a variety of rules for financing a car, and most follow a similar pattern with different limits. We recommend the 20/5/15 rule: put 20% down, finance for no more than five years, and keep all car costs at or below 15% of your gross income. All three parts work together. A car fits your budget only if you can meet all three at once. If you have to break one to make the numbers work, the car is likely more than you can comfortably afford.


**Put 20% down**
That may seem steep, but **[equity from a trade-in counts toward it](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/how-to-get-the-most-money-for-your-trade-in)** , so it may be more within reach than you think. In most states, **[a trade-in also lowers your sales tax](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/how-do-taxes-work-on-private-car-sales)** because tax is calculated on the price after the trade-in value is subtracted.


**Finance for no more than five years**
Financing over five years lowers the monthly payment enough to make today's vehicle prices more reasonable. For new-vehicle buyers, five years also lines up with the **[5-year/60,000-mile powertrain warranty](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/what-does-a-new-vehicle-warranty-cover)** many mainstream automakers offer. As long as you drive less than 12,000 miles a year, you won't be paying off a loan and a major engine or transmission repair at the same time. Used-vehicle buyers should check how much factory coverage remains, if any.


Loan terms have been extended significantly in recent years. In Q3 2026, more than a quarter of new-car loans stretch to seven years or more ([Edmunds](https://www.edmunds.com/press/new-car-financing-records-pile-up-in-q3-as-buyers-borrow-more-and-stretch-loans-longer-according-to-edmunds.html) ). Buyers should be wary of taking on a loan that long. It will generally outlast most warranty periods, total interest payments will increase significantly, and if anything happens to the vehicle in the first several years, you're likely to be underwater on the loan.


**Keep all car costs at or below 15% of gross income**
In this model, that 15% covers everything: the payment, insurance, fuel, maintenance, and registration. Running costs come out of the 15%, not on top of it. When considering financing a vehicle, it's increasingly important to account for these other costs. Modern vehicles are more complex, and both **[insurance and repair costs have increased substantially](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/what-to-expect-when-buying-a-high-mileage-car)** . In 2026, fuel prices are also up, so all of this should be taken into account.


## How is the 20/5/15 rule different from the 20/4/10 rule?


The 20/4/10 rule has long been a common starting point for a car budget. It works the same way as the 20/5/15 rule with lower limits: put 20% down, finance for no more than four years, and keep the monthly payment under 10% of your gross income. Some versions apply the 10% to the loan payment alone, while stricter versions include all vehicle expenses, such as insurance, fuel, maintenance, and registration.


But the cost of owning and operating a vehicle has climbed faster than most people's incomes, and the 20/4/10 rule has become outdated. For example, the U.S. median household income in 2025 was[$87,460](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/income-poverty-health-insurance-coverage.html) . Under the strict 20/4/10 rule, that household's monthly car budget would be $729, which would be almost entirely consumed by typical running costs. What's left would cap the vehicle price at under $7,000, a very difficult price to find these days. The 20/5/15 rule is a more realistic solution.

## What does a car really cost beyond the loan payment?


The monthly car payment is only part of your total costs. Other monthly and annual costs, such as **[insurance](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/the-beginners-guide-to-car-insurance)** , fuel, maintenance, and **[registration](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/everything-you-need-to-know-about-car-registration)** , add to your running costs. Depending on your commute, driving history, and vehicle, these costs can add several hundred dollars per month to your payment.


Depreciation never actually shows up on a receipt, but **[it's the highest cost of owning a car](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/what-to-know-about-depreciation-when-shopping-for-a-car)** , and it hits the hardest in the first months after a vehicle purchase. If you know you plan to trade in your vehicle in a few years, this is something to consider. According to Edmunds, roughly 29% of financed trade-ins were underwater in the third quarter of 2026, by an average of $7,107. Negative equity must be paid off before the title can be transferred, so owners either pay it in cash or roll it into their next loan. Rolling it over reduces the amount you can afford for your next vehicle and puts you even deeper underwater.


Depreciation matters even if you never trade in. If something happens, such as a crash or a tree falling on the vehicle during a storm, insurance will typically pay only the vehicle's current value, which may be less than what you owe on a longer loan.


## What are car buyers paying?


If it's been a few years since you last purchased a vehicle, sticker prices today will likely be substantially higher. In the third quarter of 2026, **[used-vehicle buyers averaged $582 per month](https://www.cargurus.com/shop/used)** on an average loan of $30,703. New-vehicle buyers paid a record average of $787 a month on a record average loan of $44,664, and 21.2% of them now pay more than $1,000 per month in loan payments alone, before any other costs ([Edmunds](https://www.edmunds.com/press/new-car-financing-records-pile-up-in-q3-as-buyers-borrow-more-and-stretch-loans-longer-according-to-edmunds.html) ).


### What does it take to follow the 20/5/15 rule today?


At the average used-vehicle listing price of $29,800 ( **[CarGurus Intelligence Report, October 2026](https://dealers.cargurus.com/blog/cargurus-intelligence-report---october-2026)** ), a buyer who puts 20% down and finances the rest at 10.6% for 60 months pays about $514 a month. Add an estimated $600 a month in running costs, and staying within 15% of income takes about $89,000 a year. Your actual running costs will vary depending on how much you drive, your powertrain, and other factors.


That is slightly above the $87,460 median household income, which means the average used vehicle sits just beyond what a typical household can comfortably afford under our rule.


New is further out of reach. At the average new-vehicle listing price of $51,600 and the 7.0% average new-car APR, that same buyer would pay about $817 a month, and staying within 15% of income would take about $113,000 a year. That is roughly 30% more than the median household earns.

## How does your credit score change what you can afford?


When you borrow money to buy a car, your monthly payment isn't simply the price divided by the number of months. Lenders charge interest on top of the principal (the amount you borrow). Your credit score sets your interest rate, and your interest rate sets how much car your monthly budget can buy.


Lenders sort auto-loan applicants into credit tiers based on how likely they are to repay, and they charge higher interest rates to riskier borrowers. A higher rate means a higher monthly payment, so a lower score shrinks the price range you can afford. Your rate can matter as much as the sticker price, particularly as the loan terms get longer. On those longer loans, you're likely to owe more in principal than the vehicle is worth for the first several years. For the same car and the same loan, a borrower with a higher credit score will pay less over the life of the loan than one with a lower credit score.


The effect on your budget is direct. On an $80,000 income, abiding by the 20/5/15 rule, and assuming $600 per month in running costs, you have $400 per month for the loan. Over 60 months, that $400 buys about $25,700 of used car at 6.29% and only $18,200 at 21.62%.

### What credit score gets a good auto loan rate?


The biggest jump is at the prime threshold. Moving from near prime to prime cuts the average used-car rate by more than five percentage points, which on a $30,000 loan is roughly $4,600 in interest over five years. That is more than most buyers will ever negotiate off a sticker price. If your score sits just under 661, **[raising it before you apply](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/how-financing-works-when-buying-a-car)** is the single highest-value thing you can do before you shop.


## Do longer loans make a car more affordable?


A longer loan lowers your monthly payment but raises your total cost, because you pay interest on the outstanding balance for more months. Stretching the average $30,703 used-car loan at 10.6% from 48 to 84 months reduces the monthly payment by $268 but adds about $5,800 in interest. So that $30,703 loan costs $37,804 over four years, or $43,619 over seven years.

## Why are 72- and 84-month loans risky?


Auto loans are amortized: each monthly payment first covers the interest that has built up since your last payment, and the rest goes to the principal. The payment stays the same, but the amount applied to interest versus principal changes as the balance shrinks.


Using the used-car example above, about $211 of the first $514 payment goes to interest and $303 to principal. Each month, the balance of the loan decreases, so the next month's interest charge is smaller and more of the $514 payment goes toward principal. By the final payment, interest amounts to about $4, and nearly the entire payment goes to paying off the principal. You can ask your lender for an amortization schedule to see exactly how much your principal decreases with each payment.


Longer loans pay down the principal more slowly, while a car loses value fastest in its first few years. Together, this combination can leave buyers underwater for much of the loan term.


Some buyers may be tempted to reduce the down payment and extend the loan term to afford a pricier vehicle, which is a risky move. If you do choose a longer term, a strong down payment is the best protection against negative equity.


## How do you calculate your car budget before you shop?


Start with 15% of your gross monthly income and subtract your running costs, insurance, fuel, maintenance, and registration. What's left is your maximum monthly payment. Use your preapproved rate and a term of no more than 60 months to convert that payment into a maximum loan amount. Add your down payment and trade-in equity to that loan amount to get your maximum price. Remember, this is **[your maximum all-in price](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/understanding-taxes-and-fees-when-buying-a-car)** including taxes, fees, etc. When shopping, it's important to account for all those fees due at purchase, including the destination charge. Most automakers only advertise the manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP), but the destination or delivery charge is a mandatory fee that's applied to all new vehicle purchases, and those fees have ballooned in the past few years.


**The five-step budget**


- Check credit tier
- **[Get preapproved](https://www.cargurus.com/shop/auto-financing)** to replace the average with your real rate
- Set the monthly ceiling
- Convert to a loan and price
- Negotiate the out-the-door price against that ceiling


## The Bottom Line


Online calculators, like the **[CarGurus auto loan calculator](https://www.cargurus.com/shop/auto-calculator)** , can help you narrow down what your payment will look like over different loan terms depending on your credit tier, down payment, and total loan amount. Ultimately, the right number is the total monthly cost your income supports over the full term, not the largest payment a lender will approve.


## FAQs


- What percentage of my income should go to a car payment?
- Is a $1,000 car payment too high?
- How much should I put down on a car?
- Should I buy new or used to stay on budget?
- Does getting preapproved hurt my credit score?
- Can I refinance if my rate is too high?
- What is a good APR for a car loan right now?


### What percentage of my income should go to a car payment?


We recommend keeping all car costs, including the payment, insurance, fuel and maintenance, at or below 15% of gross monthly income.


### Is a $1,000 car payment too high?


It depends on your income. Under the 20/5/15 rule, $1,000 a month (including payment, insurance, fuel and maintenance) takes a gross income of about $80,000 a year.


### How much should I put down on a car?


Twenty percent is the standard target because it offsets first-year depreciation and lowers the risk of owing more than the car is worth. Lenders rarely require a substantial down payment, which is why the discipline falls to the buyer.


### Should I buy new or used to stay on budget?


Used loans are typically smaller; however, many automakers offer incentives and better interest rates on new vehicles, and **[leasing](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/everything-you-need-to-know-about-leasing)** may afford you the most vehicle for the lowest monthly cost. Comparing total interest and running all costs, including maintenance, is better than considering the sticker price alone.


### Does getting preapproved hurt my credit score?


Buyers may get pre-qualified or pre-approved with a lender before shopping to know how much they can afford and what monthly payments they can expect. These "soft inquiries" don't impact your credit score. Even when you're ready to make a purchase, rate shopping causes little damage when done in a short window, typically between 14 and 45 days.


### Can I refinance if my rate is too high?


Yes, refinancing your auto loan may offer savings if your credit has improved since you first financed or market rates have fallen. However, a new loan may extend the term or incur fees that can wipe out those savings. Ensure that your new loan doesn't erase the savings in added interest or fees.


### What is a good APR for a car loan right now?


Your APR will depend on your credit tier and current market rates. The CarGurus **[auto loan calculator](https://www.cargurus.com/shop/auto-calculator)** can help you estimate your monthly payment and APR based on today's average rates.
